LACS 1000.attendance: Regular, on-time attendance is expected; each unexcused absence takes 1.5 points off the final grade. Illness, family emergencies and major professional opportunities can be excused with written notic
LACS 1000.lateWork: Unless an extension is granted, 5 points come off per day late, and work more than a week late gets no credit; extensions must be requested by email with a brief reason.
other: Submitting AI-generated content without the instructor's explicit permission counts as academic dishonesty.
Grade disputes must be made in writing and sent with the graded assignment for review.

components.note: 4 discussions (1 per week), 5 points each; each needs a reply to a different classmate

grading.extraCredit: Up to two 'Current Event Synopsis' pieces (about 200 words each, approved by email first) earn a maximum of 6 points, added to the lowest essay grade.

LACS 1000E.lateWork: No late film reviews or essays are accepted, with no exceptions.
other: Generative AI is strictly prohibited at every stage of the work, including preliminary steps.
Film reviews, essays and extra credit pieces need a heading with name, title and word count (essays also page numbers); unformatted work loses points.

materials.item: All course materials are posted on eLC; no textbook is named

LACS 2050.attendance: Students are expected to share views in discussion and take part in active-learning activities during lectures.
LACS 2050.lateWork: 10 percent of the assignment grade is lost for each day late (a 10-point assignment is capped at 9 points one day late, 8 points two days late).
LACS 2050.makeups: No make-up assignments or exams without previous notice; the one exception is valid justification, such as a doctor's note, given after the missed test or assignment.

objectives: Students will deepen their understanding of historical processes related to class, race, ethnicity, gender and sexuality in Latin America.
Students will learn and apply comparative methodologies for understanding the interrelated historical relationship between Latin America, Europe, and the United States.
Students will evaluate how Latin American governments and citizens interpret and address long-term and recent structural and social inequalities.
Students will compare the long-term legacy of memory, colonialism, and mestizaje in contemporary social, cultural and political processes.
Students will demonstrate in-depth knowledge of key concepts to interpret Latin American reality through research and expository writing projects.
topics: Separating Latin American and Caribbean thinkers in Latin American and Caribbean studies from European methodologies 2.
Colonialism, imperialism, and the formation of regional and national identities in resistance 3.
Indigenous theories, epistemologies, and ontologies 4.
Emancipatory projects such as Dependency theory, liberation theology, and revolution in
the mid-20th century 5.
Nationalism and national critique, with emphasis on indigenismo, criollismo, hybridity, mestizaje, and critiques 6.
The decolonial turn, with emphasis on indigenous theories, epistemologies, and ontologies 7.
Decolonial gender and feminism 8.
Neoliberal and post-neoliberal struggles and debates 9.
Popular culture and cultural critique

objectives: Students will use interdisciplinary approaches to explore selected themes in Latin America and the Caribbean, focusing on cultural identity and history.

Students will identify and research a country or topic of focus for the final project, applying the logic of scientific research to an academic or non-academic written, audiovisual, or digital Latin American and Caribbe…
Students will identify and synthesize relevant academic and non-academic LACS literature on a given historical, social, cultural, or political Latin America and the Caribbean or Latinx topic.
Students will also develop their language proficiency through primary readings in the target language as well as expository assignments and in-class debates in the target language.
Students will evaluate qualitative or quantitative data on a given historical, social, cultural, or political topic before assembling a written or digital product accessible to wider audiences.
topics: Latin America and the Caribbean in global and historical context.
Research basics in social sciences and the humanities.
Contemporary social and political issues in LAC.
Environment, development, and alternatives to development.
Nation and Pluri-nation, culture(s), and identities.
Race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality.
Economy, neoliberalism, and post-neoliberalism.
Topical country/regional studies and processes.
Regional integration and solidarity of the past and present.
Colonialism, Neocolonialism, and Multipolarity: Relations with Global North countries in historical perspective.
Student presentations of final papers and projects.
